Oakbank School
Work hard, be kind
Oakbank School
Welcome to Oakbank School. As a proud member of the Greenshaw Learning Trust, we are a community defined by a knowledge-rich culture where every student thrives. Our core values of Work Hard, Be Kind are not just slogans; they are the foundation of our collective commitment to a higher-performing school environment.
We believe that providing students with powerful knowledge is a matter of social justice. We empower our students with the "cultural capital" necessary to have genuine choices in their lives. We strive for excellence because we want our students to lead lives of opportunity. We believe in working together to ensure that our community supports one another and challenges one another to be the ‘best’ versions of ourselves, not because we have to improve, but because if we do, the potential is endless. We believe in the fidelity of our vision for students and staff, and strive to retain our moral compass when making decisions, to foster an open, inclusive and happy community at Oakbank.
Oakbank is on a journey of rapid transformation, where staff, students and parents are determined to improve the quality and experience of education for its community. Our current phase of school improvement features our entire team working together at pace to offer greater stability, more innovation and creativity. The aim is for greater consistency for all students, enabling them to manage their learning and themselves more effectively.
We are incredibly proud of our wonderful school community. We have made great strides in recent times to become a highly successful school, and we will not rest in our ambition of being the best that we possibly can be.
Mr R Gerrard Headteacher

Religious Education
Religious Education
Why is it important to study Religious Education?
Religious Education informs us of the way the world is today by looking at diverse faiths, ethics, and philosophies. Through the study of RE, you will get a chance to experience the awe-inspiring fact that moral and religious frameworks built the present, and we build the future, by studying a broad range of human beliefs and values.
What are the skills and knowledge you will learn in RE?
In RE, you will develop critical thinking, deal with complex ethical dilemmas, challenge previous perceptions, and access the philosophical ideas that will help you understand who you are and where you come from. We will explore key religious teachings—with a specific focus on Christianity and Islam for the AQA specification—and study moral issues from around the world, so you can build an awareness of the wider world.
What are the pathways and opportunities that studying RE will open both at school and beyond?
RE has many transferable skills which prepare us to challenge the origin of ethical arguments and determine their value to draw balanced conclusions. This is important because it will help you create your own informed opinions about the moral issues you encounter and build on the lessons learnt from religious and secular traditions.
These can lead to careers in law, medicine, social work, politics, journalism, education, and any career that requires the handling and organising of complex information, ethical concepts, and ideas.

Maths
Maths – Core Subject
Exam Board: Pearson Edexcel
Mathematics at Oakbank School is grounded in evidence-based teaching methodologies, drawing from the principles of Barack Rosenshine and Doug Lemov.
The department follows the MathsPad curriculum, along with other Greenshaw Learning Trust schools, which is delivered using the "I, We, You" gradual release modelling method used in all Oakbank Methods. Maths incorporates mini whiteboards through the "1, 2, 3 show me" routine for real-time assessment in every lesson.
To maximize student potential, the curriculum is tiered during Year 9 as part of an explicit drive to enter more students into the Pearson Edexcel exam board Higher tier paper. Learning is supported outside the classroom by weekly Sparx Maths homework, which features a self-guided component that rewards students for completing optional practice. All mathematical methods used in lessons can be found in the departmental method book {link needed}
Sparx
Sparx Maths is an online platform used to support maths learning by combining digital practice with physical written work in a notebook.
Sparx creates a strategically chosen homework task for each student every week. The questions adapt to the student's ability level so that they can achieve a 100 percent completion rate. Each homework assignment includes a mix of current and past topics to help students remember what they have previously learned. If a student gets stuck on a problem, they can watch a short instructional video attached to that exact question. Students can also choose to complete optional, harder practice to stretch themselves and earn extra experience points.
Sparx is due every Monday and followed by an in-class assessment to consolidate student learning.

Science
Science – Core Subject
Science at Oakbank is a core part of our offer, offering biology, chemistry and physics at Foundation and Higher Level.
Sparx Science
The Sparx Science platform is an online homework tool designed to help students remember, understand, and apply what they learn in school. It automatically sets weekly science homework that matches exactly what your child is learning in class across biology, chemistry, and physics.
Sparx Science helps students by adapting to their individual learning levels. If a student is struggling, the system makes the questions more accessible by using word banks and multiple-choice options to help build their confidence. For students who are doing well, it automatically unlocks harder questions that challenge them to solve complex problems and prepare for GCSE exams.
Sparx Science is also designed to catch common science mistakes, like confusing mass with weight. When it notices a student making a typical mistake, it stops and gives them instant feedback to correct the misunderstanding before it becomes a bad habit.
Sparx is due every week.
Curriculum Map
The science curriculum at Oakbank School is designed to foster a sense of curiosity about the natural world by guiding students from concrete, observable phenomena to abstract scientific systems. In Year 7, students begin by exploring the immediate mechanics of life through cells, organisation, and body systems, which satisfies their natural curiosity about how their own bodies function. This understanding is expanded in Year 8 as they study ecosystems, photosynthesis, and climate systems, shifting their perspective to global interactions and the wider environment. By Key Stage 4, this curiosity is directed toward microscopic and unseen forces, such as the chemical and biological pathways of bioenergetics or the invisible fields governing magnetism and electromagnetism.

Art
Art
Why is it important to study Art?
Studying Art is crucial as it nurtures creativity, critical thinking, and emotional expression, benefiting personal growth and practical skill development. By exploring art history, design elements, and cultural influences, students deepen their understanding of societal evolution and cultural heritage, fostering an appreciation for diverse viewpoints. Creating art allows individuals to uniquely express thoughts and emotions, while also enhancing observational skills and visual literacy, enabling a deeper interpretation of the world around them.
Furthermore, at Oakbank, Art develops confidence and resilience through encouraging experimentation and problem-solving in creative processes. Exposure to global artistic traditions and contemporary issues promotes empathy and cultural sensitivity, facilitating deeper connections with others and broadening understanding of different cultural perspectives.
What are the skills and knowledge you will learn in Art?
Studying Art equips you with a range of practical skills and knowledge. You'll learn different artistic techniques like drawing, painting, sculpture, and digital art. Understanding elements of design such as line, shape, colour, and texture helps you express your personal style and create visually appealing artwork. Exploring art history deepens your appreciation for cultural contexts and artistic styles over time.
Art at Oakbank School also fosters creativity and problem-solving abilities as you experiment with different materials and ideas. These skills are valuable not only for personal expression but also for future careers. Overall, studying Art enhances your ability to create, understand, and appreciate art in diverse forms and contexts.
What are the pathways and opportunities that studying Art will open both at school and beyond?
Studying Art at Oakbank offers numerous opportunities both during and after school. Starting your artistic journey in Year 7, you can advance through GCSE and A-Level courses if desired. Art education prepares students for careers in various fields such as Art, Design, Graphic and Visual Design, Education, Illustration, Curation, Restoration and Conservation, Art History, Research, Freelancing, and Art Entrepreneurship. Graduates can pursue paths in museums, galleries, or establish their own art-related ventures. Additionally, Art supports disciplines like art therapy and charitable projects, fostering critical thinking and creativity essential in any profession.
Art will be a Choice for Year 2026-27 Year 10 Students

English
English - Core Subject
English at Oakbank School is a serious, but also joyous and intellectually fulfilling pursuit, leading to a suite of modern careers in the UK and beyond. English enrichment is supported through spelling bees, creative contests and a relentless celebration of our beautiful, complex language and national culture.
English at Oakbank School is unapologetically ambitious for all students and encourages strong elocution, critical thinking and literacy. English staff support all students to become strong independent readers and writers and access the best universities and vocational colleges of their choosing.
Sparx Reader (KS3)
Sparx Reader is a fantastic reading platform for KS3 students, completed every week.
The implementation of this platform is a direct strategy to combat the Matthew Effect in education, a phenomenon where the rich get richer and the poor get poorer based on their reading skills. In a literacy context, fluent readers who enjoy reading read more, which expands their vocabulary and cognitive skills, making reading even easier. Conversely, struggling readers read less, causing the gap between them and their peers to widen exponentially over time. Sparx Reader disrupts this negative cycle by ensuring every student, regardless of their starting point, engages in a baseline of successful, regular reading practice that fosters upward growth.
Initially, the platform assesses each student to determine their specific reading age and comprehension capability, providing a personalised library of e-books tailored precisely to their level. This ensures that every student is reading books that are accessible enough to prevent frustration, yet challenging enough to expand their vocabulary and improve their overall literacy skills. Unlike traditional reading logs which can be easily falsified, Sparx Reader ensures that meaningful reading is actually taking place. As students read through the digital text, the platform introduces quick, strategic multiple-choice questions at logical points in the story. These comprehension checks assess whether the student is focusing on the narrative rather than skimming or skipping pages. If a student tries to rush through the text, they will fail the checks and be required to re-read the section, reinforcing the value of careful, deliberate reading.
Sparx Reader is due for completion every week and students are expected to reach 300 points.
Curriculum Map
The English curriculum map is strategically engineered to optimise long-term knowledge retention by aligning its revision and retrieval intervals with the Ebbinghaus forgetting curve, ensuring that critical concepts are deliberately spaced, interleaved, and revisited across the academic years before cognitive decay occurs.
KS4 is founded on an exploration of the specification's core texts, which are introduced sequentially and then systematically revisited: the 19th-century prose of A Christmas Carol is studied in Year 10 and consolidated in Year 11, the Shakespearean tragedy of Macbeth in term 4 of Year 10, the thematic complexities within the Conflict Poetry Anthology transition from Year 10 into Year 11, and the modern drama of An Inspector Calls completes the core text cycle at the end of Year 10.
A robust and highly enjoyable Key Stage 3 framework purposefully builds upwards to Key Stage 4. This is evidenced by the deliberate mapping of foundational skills: early exploration of William Blake's poetry, War Poetry, and Gothic Fiction in Key Stage 3 acts as a direct conceptual runway for the complex Power and Conflict poetry anthology and 19th-century text requirements at GCSE, ensuring students transition to their terminal Year 11 examinations with mature, deeply embedded competencies. These competencies support the Language Papers, which are designed to test fluency of foundational reading and analysis skills.

Geography
Geography
Why is it important to study Geography?
The Geography curriculum in both KS3 and 4 aims to develop pupils so that they become inquisitive and confident learners. It will foster an understanding of students’ roles within society, on a local, regional, national and global scale and the impact they as individuals have upon the environment. We aim to promote an understanding of the opportunities and challenges that people have in relation to their social, economic and environmental impacts. The curriculum will nurture the skills needed in evaluation to develop reasoning for sustainable management strategies which can be used to adapt and mitigate the challenges our world faces in the future.
What are the skills and knowledge you will learn in Geography?
Geography is unique as it offers opportunities to conduct fieldwork investigations in and around the local area. This will develop skills in areas such as:
Data Collection, presentation and analysis
Statistical analysis
In addition to this, the course will also develop the following skills:
Information Communication Technology
Global perspectives.
What are the pathways and opportunities that studying Geography will open both at school and beyond?
Geography offers opportunities for many career paths and, as a “facilitating subject” as defined by the leading Russell Group of universities, is well regarded by institutions of higher education and employers. Careers for geographers split into the following broad groups: leisure & culture; travel; environment & sustainability; the business world; development & global issues; settlement & planning (e.g. housing manager, town planner); social occupations (e.g. teacher, HR, market research); physical systems (e.g. hydrologist) and occupations based on geographical techniques (e.g. cartography, developing GIS).

History
Why is it important to study History?
History informs us of the way the world is today by looking at previous events. Through the study of history, you will get a chance to experience the awe-inspiring fact that our ancestors built the present, and we build the future, by studying a broad range of human history.
What are the skills and knowledge you will learn in History?
In History, you will develop critical thinking, deal with misinformation, challenge previous perceptions and access the stories in history that will help you understand who you are and where you come from. We will explore British topics and study events from around the world, so you can build an awareness of the wider world.
What are the pathways and opportunities that studying History will open both at school and beyond?
History has many transferable skills which prepare us to challenge the origin of information and determine its value to draw conclusions. This is important because it will help you create your own informed opinions about the information you encounter and build on the lessons learnt from the past.
These can lead to historical academia, archaeology, politics, law and any career that requires the handling and organising of complex information, concepts and ideas.
Curriculum Map
Our history curriculum builds a deep knowledge of the past by organizing historical events into a logical, step-by-step timeline over five years. In Year 7, students focus on the foundations of England, learning how Roman, Anglo-Saxon, Viking, and Norman invasions shaped the island. Year 8 introduces broader global themes, focusing on the rise and fall of major empires and the economic shifts of the Industrial Revolution. In Year 9, the focus moves to modern global conflicts, including World War One, World War Two, and the Cold War. This timeline provides the essential background knowledge students need for their Year 10 and 11 GCSE studies, where they revisit these eras in much greater depth to analyze British migration, Elizabethan England, and Weimar Germany. This curriculum directly supports and reinforces fundamental British values through its specific choice of topics.

Careers Overview
Careers Overview
At Oakbank we are committed to equipping our students with the knowledge, tools and skills to enable them to make informed decisions about their future careers.
Oakbank wants all young people to leave with an ambitious, achievable, career goal; and the knowledge of how to get there.
Students can use the Careers Education Information Advice & Guidance (CEIAG) provision within the school, which is delivered through our Personal Development programme of PSHE lessons, assemblies as well as specific Careers and Work-Related Learning activities. Our careers resources are consistently updated and developed to provide a quality careers area that is available to all students.
Our Careers Lead in school is Ms A Korporowicz. Please do get in touch if you have any specific career queries via
akorporowicz@oakbankschool.co.uk
Gatsby Benchmarks
The Charitable foundation, Gatsby, commissioned Sir John Holman to examine what could be done to improve career guidance in England’s secondary schools. After international research, judgements were made on what “good” careers guidance looked like. These judgements are in the form of eight benchmarks, identifying different dimensions of good career guidance. The benchmarks are summarised in the table below. These benchmarks underpin and run through the careers programme at Oakbank School.
A stable careers programme
Every school and college should have an embedded programme of career education and guidance that is known and understood by pupils, parents, teachers, governors and employers.
Learning from career and labour market information
Every pupil, and their parents, should have access to good quality information about future study options and labour market opportunities. They will need the support of an informed adviser to make best use of available information.
Addressing the needs of each pupil Pupils have different career guidance needs at different stages.
Opportunities for advice and support need to be tailored to the needs of each pupil. A school’s careers programme should embed equality and diversity considerations throughout.
Linking curriculum learning to careers
All teachers should link curriculum learning with careers. STEM subject teachers should highlight the relevance of STEM subjects for a wide range of future career paths.
Encounters with employers and employees
Every pupil should have multiple opportunities to learn from employers about work, employment and the skills that are valued in the workplace. This can be through a range of enrichment activities including visiting speakers, mentoring and enterprise schemes.
Experiences of workplaces
Every pupil should have first-hand experiences of the workplace through work visits, work shadowing and/or work experience to help their exploration of career opportunities, and expand their networks.
Encounters with further and higher education
All pupils should understand the full range of learning opportunities that are available to them. This includes both academic and vocational routes and learning in schools, colleges, universities and in the workplace
Every pupil should have opportunities for guidance interviews with a career adviser, who could be internal (a member of school staff) or external, provided they are trained to an appropriate level. These should be available whenever significant study or career choices are being made. They should be expected for all pupils but should be timed to meet their individual needs.
Our young people have access to a wide range of opportunities over different year groups to learn about different careers and the employability skills required to get them. These include:
The school uses drop-down days (where the school timetable is suspended), personal development time and assembly time to deliver these.

Who do we work with?
One of our close partners for the Career Programme is:
Study Higher is a network of universities within our region, working together to deliver outreach activities to young people with the aim of helping them make strong decisions about their future. The outreach is aimed at students in Years 9-13.
Oakbank is a target school for Study Higher and we have the support of a Higher Education Liaison Officer (Joanna Ridley) and access to a wide range of activities and resources to support our careers program. All Study Higher activities are free of charge to the school and to participating students.
We have developed links with the Universities of Reading, Surrey and Oxford Brooks. We are have worked closely with local businesses through the Hire Power event. We have had the British Army and the NHS in this academic year.

Career Pilot
It is our aim to get all students an account set up on Career Pilot - a free, award-winning, careers website www.careerpilot.org.uk. It is for young people and of a Parent Zone aimed at helping parents and carers get the information they need to help their children make the right choices at 14, 16, and 18. The site is managed by the Western Vocational Progression Consortium and funded through a partnership of 20 universities.
The Careerpilot website aims to provide 13-19-year-olds in the South of England with information on the full range of choices available at 14, 16 and 18, including apprenticeships, college, higher-level study, etc.
